text:
And now you may think whatever evil you please of us Cavaliers, but toward that woman there we have done all the good we could. And it is thanks to her that we have not shot every last one of you dead tonight. But now I tell you: set her free and go your way, or else I believe the earth will open and swallow you up! And when you leave here, ask God to forgive you for having frightened and grieved one who is so good and innocent! And now be off with you! We have had enough of you!

Long before he had finished speaking, those who had carried the Countess out had set her down on one of the stone steps, and now a large peasant came forward to her quite deliberately and held out his great hand.

“Thank you and good night!” he said. “We meant the Countess no harm, Countess.”

After him came another and gave her hand a gentle squeeze.

“Thank you and good night! The Countess must not be angry with us!”

Gösta jumped down and took his place at her side. Then they shook his hand as well.

And now they came forward, slow and stolid, one by one, to bid the two of them good night before they left. They were subdued once more; once more they were human beings, as they had been when they left their homes that morning, before hunger and vengeance had turned them into wild beasts.

They looked the Countess straight in the face, and Gösta noticed how the sight of the innocence and piety they saw there brought tears to many eyes. In all of them there was a silent adoration of the noblest thing they had ever beheld. They were human beings rejoicing that one of them possessed so great a love for goodness.

Of course, not everyone could shake hands with her. There were so terribly many of them, and the young woman was tired and weak. But all of them had to come up and see her, and then they could shake Gösta’s hand; his arms could surely withstand the shaking.

Gösta stood as though in a dream. That evening, a new love welled up in his heart.

“Oh, my people,” he thought, “oh, my people, how I love you!” He felt how he loved that whole multitude as it withdrew into the darkness of the night, with the dead girl at the head of the procession—all those people in coarse clothes and foul-smelling shoes, all those who lived in the gray cottages at the edge of the forest, all those who could not wield a pen and often could not read either, all those who did not know the fullness and richness of life, only the struggle for their daily bread.

He loved them with a painful, burning tenderness that forced tears into his eyes. He did not know what he wanted to do for them, but he loved them, each and every one, with their faults and vices and frailties. Oh, Lord God, if only the day might come when he too would be loved by them!

He awoke from his dream. His wife laid her hand on his arm. The people were gone. They were alone on the steps.

“Oh, Gösta, Gösta, how could you?”

She covered her face with her hands and wept.

“What I said is true,” he exclaimed. “I never promised the girl from Nygård that I would marry her. ‘Come here next Friday, and you shall see something amusing!’ was all I said to her. I cannot help it that she was fond of me.”

“Oh, that was not it! But how could you tell the people that I was good and pure? Gösta, Gösta, do you not know that I loved you when I was not yet permitted to do so? I was ashamed before the people, Gösta. I wanted to die of shame.”

And she was shaken by sobs.

He stood looking at her.

“Oh, my friend, my beloved!” he said softly. “How fortunate you are to be so good! How fortunate you are to have so beautiful a soul within you!”

CHAPTER THIRTY-THREE

Kevenhüller

In the 1770s, the man who would later become the learned and accomplished Kevenhüller was born in Germany. He was the son of a burgrave and could have lived in lofty castles and ridden at the Emperor’s side if he had wished, but he did not.

He would have liked to fasten windmill sails to the castle’s highest tower, turn the knights’ hall into a fine metalworker’s shop and the women’s chamber into a clockmaker’s workshop. He would have liked to fill the castle with spinning wheels and working levers. But since such things could not be done, he left all the splendor behind and apprenticed himself to a clockmaker. There he learned everything there was to learn about cogwheels, springs, and pendulums. He learned to make sundials and astronomical clocks, mantel clocks with chirping canaries and shepherds blowing horns, clockworks that filled an entire church tower with their strange machinery, and watches so small that they could be set in a locket.

When he had received his master’s certificate, he put his knapsack on his back, took his knotted cudgel in hand, and wandered from place to place to study everything that ran on rollers and wheels. Kevenhüller was no ordinary clockmaker; he wanted to become a great inventor and reformer of the world.

After he had thus traveled through many countries, he also made his way to Värmland to study mill wheels and the arts of mining. One beautiful summer morning, it happened that he was crossing the market square in Karlstad. But at that same lovely hour of the morning, the Lady of the Forest had seen fit to extend her wanderings all the way into the town. The tall lady was also crossing the square, but from the opposite direction, and so she met Kevenhüller.

What a meeting for a journeyman clockmaker! She had shining green eyes and thick, pale hair that almost reached the ground, and she was dressed in shimmering green silk. Troll and heathen though she was, she was more beautiful than all the Christian women Kevenhüller had ever seen. He stood as though possessed and stared at her as she came toward him.

She came straight from the thickets in the forest’s deepest heart, where the ferns grow as tall as trees, where the gigantic pines shut out the sunlight so that it can fall only in golden flecks upon the yellow moss, and where the twinflower creeps over lichen-covered stones.

I would certainly have liked to be in Kevenhüller’s place so that I might see her as she came, with fern leaves and spruce needles tangled in her thick hair and a small black viper around her neck. Imagine her, supple in her gait as a wild animal and bringing with her a fresh scent of resin and wild strawberries, of twinflower and moss!

How the people must have stared at her when she took it into her head to walk across Karlstad’s market square! Horses must have bolted in fright at her long hair flying in the summer wind. Street urchins ran after her. The men dropped steelyard and meat axe to gape at her. The women ran screaming for the bishop and cathedral chapter to drive the unholy creature out of the town.
